article.title: Why I Started Judging the Judges: The Election That Changed How I Vote
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. When I watched a tough-on-crime prosecutor reinvent himself before a room full of progressive voters, I realized how little we really knew about the people we were electing to the bench. That experience eventually led me to create LA Progressive's Judging the Judges series. Every election season, millions of Americans confront a familiar problem. They are asked to make decisions about candidates they know almost nothing about. Nowhere is this problem more apparent than in judicial elections. Most voters can tell you something about the candidates running for president, governor, or mayor. They may have heard them speak, watched them debate, or read about their positions on issues that matter to them. But when they reach the judicial contests on their ballots, the information often disappears. There are names. There are ballot designations. Occasionally, there are carefully crafted candidate statements. But there is precious little that tells voters how these individuals think, how they have exercised power, or what kind of judgment they bring to decisions that can alter people's lives. For years, I was one of those voters. I understood the importance of the judiciary. I understood that judges make consequential decisions about incarceration, family separation, housing, civil rights, and the application of the law. Yet when I looked at the judicial candidates on my ballot, I frequently knew almost nothing about them. Then something happened that changed my approach to judicial elections. Two Encounters With the Same Prosecutor More than a dozen years ago, I had been summoned for jury duty. During jury selection, I listened to a prosecutor whose presentation struck me as decidedly tough on crime. His tone and approach left an impression. Although I was not ultimately selected to serve on the jury, I remembered him. A short time later, I encountered that same prosecutor again. This time, he was running for a seat on the Los Angeles County Superior Court. He came to speak at my local Democratic club, an organization with a reputation for being a progressive bastion. What struck me was the contrast. The prosecutor I had observed during jury selection presented one face of himself in the courtroom. The judicial candidate standing before my fellow Democratic club members presented a decidedly different one. The courtroom prosecutor had emphasized a tough-on-crime approach. The candidate seeking the support of progressive voters sounded quite different. I couldn't ignore the disconnect. Perhaps both presentations reflected genuine aspects of his professional outlook. Prosecutors and judicial candidates operate in different settings, with different responsibilities. But the contrast raised a question I could not shake: How could voters know who they were really electing if they encountered candidates only in carefully managed campaign settings? My fellow club members had not necessarily seen what I had seen in that courtroom. They were evaluating the candidate based on his presentation to them. I had the unusual advantage of having observed him in a different professional setting. And it occurred to me that this was precisely the problem with judicial elections. Most voters never get to see candidates exercising the authority they already possess. They rarely observe them prosecuting cases, representing clients, ruling on motions, negotiating pleas, or interacting with the people whose lives are caught up in the justice system. Instead, voters encounter a campaign version of a professional whose record may be difficult to examine. That realization became the foundation of LA Progressive's Judging the Judges series. The Problem Isn't That Voters Don't Care I've been thinking a great deal about why Americans don't vote. Research shows that some nonvoters are discouraged by the available candidates, some believe their participation will make little difference, and others face practical barriers involving work, transportation, health, or family responsibilities. But there is another explanation that deserves greater attention: Sometimes people don't vote because they don't have enough information to make a responsible choice. Judicial elections illustrate that problem particularly well. When someone leaves a judicial contest blank, it's more likely than not that they don't know anything about the candidate. I understand that predicament because I experienced it myself. The distinction matters. If someone doesn't care about an election, persuading them to participate may require changing their sense of political engagement. But if someone wants to participate and lacks information, the immediate problem is different. They need access to credible, understandable research. That is a problem journalists can help address. Judicial Elections Demand More Than a Campaign Biography California's judicial elections are especially challenging. Superior Court judges serve six-year terms. Many first reach the bench through gubernatorial appointment, and uncontested incumbents generally do not appear on the ballot. When voters do face a contested judicial election, the candidates frequently have considerably lower public profiles than candidates for legislative or executive office. Yet the consequences of judicial decisions are anything but obscure. Judges decide whether people remain incarcerated while awaiting trial. They make rulings that can affect the admissibility of evidence, the conduct of criminal proceedings, child custody, civil disputes, and the protection of constitutional rights. Their work is not abstract. For someone facing the loss of freedom, housing, or family relationships, the person sitting on the bench can have an enormous impact. A judicial candidate's campaign presentation cannot tell us everything we need to know about how that person will exercise such authority. Neither can a résumé listing years of experience. Experience matters. Legal knowledge matters. Professional competence matters. But so do judicial temperament, fairness, impartiality, and a demonstrated commitment to applying the law faithfully. Those qualities deserve careful examination. Building Judging the Judges The experience with that prosecutor motivated me to begin researching judicial candidates rather than accepting the limited information placed before voters. That work developed into LA Progressive's Judging the Judges series. The series has appeared across multiple election cycles, with published installments dating back at least to 2008 and continuing through the 2026 elections. Over the years, our work has drawn on judicial candidate evaluations, public records, professional backgrounds, available interviews, and other sources that can help voters understand the people seeking seats on the bench. The goal has been to make judicial elections less mysterious. Research does not eliminate disagreement. Two informed people can review the same judicial candidate's record and reach different conclusions. And no amount of research can perfectly predict how someone will perform as a judge. But voters should not have to confront these elections armed with little more than a candidate's name and ballot designation. The public deserves accessible information about the professional experience, qualifications, and records of those seeking judicial authority. That belief continues to guide the series. What Voter Abstention Taught Me About Journalism The broader debate about voter participation has reinforced something I learned from that first experience. We often talk about voting as though the entire burden rests on the individual. Citizens are told that they have a responsibility to study the issues, research the candidates, and participate in elections. There is merit in that expectation. But what responsibility do our political institutions, news organizations, and civic associations bear for ensuring that meaningful information is available? Democracy asks citizens to exercise judgment. That judgment requires knowledge. And knowledge is not distributed equally. People with professional connections, legal expertise, flexible schedules, and access to political networks may have advantages in learning about candidates that other voters do not. Even someone who follows politics closely can struggle to find reliable information about judicial races. That information gap has consequences. When voters know little about the candidates, endorsements, ballot designations, name recognition, and campaign resources can assume greater importance. Those signals may provide useful information, but they are not substitutes for examining a candidate's professional record. This is also why I resist the easy characterization of nonvoters as apathetic. A voter who leaves a judicial race blank because the available information is inadequate has identified a real democratic problem. The answer cannot simply be to shame that person for not voting. We must also ask why such an important election presents such a difficult information challenge in the first place. From Frustration to Information I have never found a particularly convincing argument that simply staying home on Election Day will, by itself, improve our political system. I understand why people become frustrated. I understand why they lose confidence in candidates and institutions. And I understand why someone might refuse to cast a vote in a race where they cannot make an informed choice. But refusing to participate does not automatically produce a more accountable political system. Nor does casting an uninformed vote necessarily improve democracy. What I learned from my encounters with that prosecutor was that there is another response to the problem: investigate. Ask questions. Look beyond the campaign presentation. Examine the available record. Compare what candidates say with what they have actually done. Make the information accessible to others. That is what Judging the Judges grew out of. I did not begin researching judicial candidates because I believed I had all the answers. I began because I realized how much I didn't know. And because I had witnessed firsthand how differently the same candidate could present himself in a courtroom and before a room of progressive voters. That experience transformed a personal frustration into an ongoing publishing project. Years later, the lesson remains just as important. A democracy cannot reasonably expect informed participation while leaving voters uninformed about the people asking to exercise power over their lives. If we want to understand why people don't vote, we should certainly listen to their explanations. But we should also examine what we are asking them to do—and whether we have given them the tools to do it responsibly. For me, that inquiry began with jury duty, a prosecutor, and an unexpected second encounter at a Democratic club. It continues with every edition of Judging the Judges . California Judicial Elections: Research Resources These resources provide information about California Superior Court judicial candidates, including professional qualifications, disciplinary histories, courtroom conduct, campaign contributions, and voter guides. Los Angeles-specific sources are identified. Bar association evaluations and qualifications 1. Los Angeles County Bar Association (LACBA) — Judicial candidate evaluations and qualification ratings for Los Angeles Superior Court races. 2. State Bar of California — Attorney Search — Attorney licensing, years of practice, professional standing, and public disciplinary records. 3. State Bar — Judicial Nominees Evaluation Commission — Explains how candidates for gubernatorial judicial appointment are evaluated. Individual evaluations generally remain confidential. Judicial performance and courtroom conduct 4. The Robing Room — User-submitted reviews of judges, including California Superior Court judges. Reviews are anecdotal and should be independently verified. 5. California Commission on Judicial Performance — Official records of public judicial discipline and misconduct findings. 6. Los Angeles Superior Court — Judicial Officers — Current judicial assignments, departments, and courthouse information. 7. La Defensa — Court Watch LA — Courtroom accountability research, judicial observations, and judicial election materials. Court decisions and public records 8. California Courts — Judicial Opinions — Published appellate decisions, including decisions reviewing Superior Court rulings. 9. CourtListener — Searchable opinions and court records, including selected California cases. 10. Trellis Law — California trial court records, judicial rulings, and case information. Some features require payment. Campaign finance and candidate information 11. Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder — Official candidate information, election records, and voter information guides. 12. Los Angeles County Campaign Finance Portal — Judicial campaign contributions, expenditures, and financial disclosures. 13. California Secretary of State — Power Search — Searchable campaign finance information for committees filing at the state level. Many Superior Court campaigns file locally. California judicial election voter guides and reporting 14. LAist — 2026 Los Angeles Superior Court Judicial Guide — Candidate biographies, State Bar profiles, LACBA ratings, and candidate questionnaires. 15. LAist — How LACBA Evaluates Judicial Candidates — Explains the bar association's methodology and how to interpret its ratings. 16. La Defensa — November 2026 Voter Guide — Detailed research on Los Angeles Superior Court candidates, courtroom accountability, and the organization's endorsements. 17. Los Angeles Times — 2026 Superior Court Judicial Guide — Candidate experience, professional qualifications, and competitive judicial races. 18.
